A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. The model renaming and relocated material can be matched. A duplicated dataset heading in v3 Table 3 creates a localized reporting ambiguity.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy, intervention, causal-structure, blocking, and regularization-ablation results on Checkmark, dSprites, and CelebA in Section 5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds CIFAR-10 experiments, synthetic-benchmark analyses, computational measurements, and counterfactual examples in Section 4 and Appendices H–I.

M1.justification: Causal CEM is renamed Causal CGM, but the encoder, concept copies, embedding aggregation, adjacency learning, training objectives, unfolding, and intervention procedures are retained. v1's neural parametrization and unfolding descriptions move to v3 Appendices D–E; the CaCE regularizer already appeared in v1 Appendix B.4.

E1.justification: v3 adds CIFAR-10 with automatically extracted concepts and a synthetic tabular benchmark with controllable concept incompleteness (Appendices G.1 and H.4–H.6). These extend coverage beyond the original three datasets to automatically annotated images and systematically incomplete concept information.

E2.justification: Black box, CBM, and CEM remain the evaluated baselines. The renamed supplied-graph +CD variant remains in corresponding original experiments. New benchmark comparisons reuse these methods; +CD is unavailable on CIFAR-10 because of stated computational cost, rather than being removed from an existing comparison.

E3.justification: Additional protocols measure concept-only intervention accuracy, vary synthetic concept counts across 10/30/60/100 and incompleteness across 0/0.1/0.5/0.9, compare one to three unfolding steps, and measure parameters and training/inference time. CIFAR-10 receives a 25-epoch budget. The documented protocols for the original benchmarks are retained.

E4.justification: The original CaCE-regularization ablations remain. v3 adds controlled concept-incompleteness tests, computational scaling analysis, and an unfolding-depth ablation in H.4–H.6. It also adds concept-only intervention analysis, explicit CelebA counterfactual examples, and broader PNS analysis, substantially expanding examination of robustness and model behavior.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five seeds, 1–5, and retain the existing uncertainty-reporting practices. v3 Appendix I newly explains that unidentifiable PNS queries yield intervals, and Figure 17 explicitly reports upper bounds. This adds identification-uncertainty reporting; no increase in repeated runs or new significance testing is documented.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 scores and regularization-ablation values are retained. New CIFAR-10 label accuracies are 93.32±0.03 for Causal CGM, 94.85±0.03 for black box, 92.17±0.11 for CBM, and 92.04±0.06 for CEM. Numerous intervention, incompleteness, scaling, unfolding, and counterfactual results are added. The added blocking-results column has an ambiguous duplicated CelebA heading.

T1.justification: v3 introduces Theorem 3.2 and its Appendix C proof concerning replacement of copy-variable parents by endogenous parents, invoking identical variables and full observability. It also adds computational-complexity and k-step-unfolding arguments. v1's cyclic and dissected PGM definitions remain in Appendix B, so their relocation is not a theoretical removal.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: causal transparency by design, competitive predictive performance, improved intermediate and downstream predictions through interventions, and support for causal reasoning and verification. Renaming and reordering these contributions do not materially change their scientific scope.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's existing distinction between model inference and real-world causality, v3 explicitly discusses non-identifiability of learned graphs, interval-valued PNS, computational tradeoffs, and CIFAR-10 intervention failures attributed to out-of-distribution embeddings. These additions materially expand the interpretation of results and the stated applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a code-repository link, CIFAR-10 training and workstation details, and updated total/reproduction compute estimates of 60/8 hours versus 40/2 hours. Most existing implementation information is retained. Appendix G.4 still promises a future code release, so actual repository availability is not established by the PDFs.

R1.justification: v3 removes several general XAI and feature-attribution references and adds sources on opacity, causal bounds, CIFAR-10, and the synthetic benchmark. Appendix K explicitly distinguishes the approach from causal representation learning. The central positioning relative to CBMs, causal discovery, and post-hoc surrogate explanations remains consistent with v1.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten around Pearl's hierarchy and CBM assumptions. The method narrative is reorganized, with derivation, neural parametrization, and unfolding moved into separate appendices; causal reasoning becomes Section 3.4 and the conclusion becomes a standalone section. Terminology changes throughout from Causal CEM to Causal CGM.

P2.justification: v3 expands Table 1 with CIFAR-10 and transparency columns, restructures the opening schematic, and adds equivalence diagrams, concept-only intervention plots, counterfactual tables, scaling/incompleteness plots, and PNS heatmaps. Existing figures and tables are resized, regrouped, or relocated within a substantially revised page layout.

improvement.justification: v1's evaluation lacked direct tests of incomplete concepts and computational scaling and used relatively small annotated concept sets. v3 addresses these important applicability gaps through CIFAR-10 with automatic concepts and controlled incompleteness, scaling, and unfolding experiments. Explicit counterfactual examples and new limitations also make the evidence easier to assess. Reporting weaknesses remain, including Table 3's duplicated heading and sparse details for the new synthetic experiments, but the added validation substantially strengthens the paper.
